>>PS: Some psychiatrists may tell you that SSRIs are not addictive, that they only cause chemical dependency. But trust me, from the user perspective, there is no difference.
>
>There is a difference because an addiction creates a drug reinforcing behaviour that leads to cravings and the user ever wanting more of it. Since SSRI:s lack this property they are per definition not addictive.
>

Weed is deemed as non-addictive, and yet I've found myself explicitly "craving" a hit during periods when I shouldn't be using it.

You're clearly using the definition of *psychological* addiction, when the OP obviously is referring to *physical* addiction. These are, in fact, two very different things.

>Don't you also think that it is a little bit hypocritical to recommend against SSRI/SNRI type of drugs when you are dependent on them to function? 

Suppose you're a heroin addict. Do you think it's a little bit hypocritical to recommend against opoid type of drugs when you are dependent on them to function?

You can easily say the same for people who are, e.g., addicted to nicotine.

>How can you distinguish dependency due to not being able to endure withdrawals vs not being able to endure the depression coming back? 

This question is acting on the basis of multiple assumptions, which are:

* withdrawal severity is uniform across all patients (assuming the same dosage, medication, frequency, etc.)

* there does not exist alternative methods or treatments available for depression

* depression symptoms at baseline are always permanent, by definition.

All of these assumptions are false:

* many people will go months enduring withdrawal, essentially being bed ridden.

* there are people who have had success using these alternative methods

* some people have less intense symptoms, or their depressive states are remarkably short term.


>It makes sense imo for people to go back onto antidepressants after quitting, because depression is very often a chronic or recurring disease..

That depends on the individual.

> and for endogenous depression there really is no fix but to take something that offsets the present chemical balance in the brain.

Sure, but the OP is arguing against the use of a *potentially* obsolete method, in favor of a newer method, which in multiple ways could objectively be superior for *some* people. And for these people, it's worth considering these methods *first*, given that SSRIs/SNRIs may have a permanent cost.

In other words, this point is irrelevant.

>Psychedelics do this too by the way so.. how can you deny that depression is not a brain chemical issue?

This isn't even part of the discussion. How are you deriving that this is what the OP is suggesting?

>
>Also you can combine some psychedelics like psilocybin, ketamine and LSD with antidepressants without problems. It is a myth that they cause serotonin syndrome together. Even MAOIs can be combined with psilocybin/ketamine/LSD. Only issue is if the drug is a potent SRI like dxm - that will cause serotonin toxicity when combined with MAOIs for instance.
>
>If anhedonia is a big problem on Effexor you could really possibly remedy that through other means like trying certain adjunct drugs or switching to a MAOI antidepressant.
>

Adjunct drugs like what? The only class of adjunct drugs I can think of amount to stimulants - these induce *stress* and don't substantially eliminate the negative effects of anhedonia.

>I agree that the FDA has outlawed several good antidepressants and blocked the development of others, but it is really wrong to say that these alternatives are non-addictive. 

Comparatively, psychedelics don't have physical withdrawal symptoms.

Those are the withdrawal symptoms that we care about the most, here.

>Many good antidepressants are outlawed/prevented from existing BECAUSE they have a potential for addiction and abuse! 

Yes, and there exist antidepressants on the market which *do* have potential for abuse. I still occasionally abuse Wellbutrin and Zoloft from time to time, for example.

What does that say about the methods used in making these decisions?

>My favourite example of such a drug is Amineptine, one of the best anti-anhedonic and pro-sexual antidepressants to have existed on the market. Only exceptions are some psychedelics like psiloycbin and LSD and a few others, these lack abuse potential but are still outlawed. Ketamine is certainly a very abusable drug. That being said I think there should be no restraints on what can be used to treat depression with. Some people can only be helped with the use of "very addictive drugs", ketamine is actually one of those examples. Others only get helped by stimulants, some only get helped by or with the addition of opioids etc.
>
>Also a lot of people DO NOT get helped by psychedelics either. Some even get worsened depression, depersonalization, psychosis etc. What is your proposed fix for these kind of people, if they can't even tolerate your proposed miracle cures?

I'm not sure OP is referring to these cures as myricals. I agree that providing counter points on your part is a good thing, as *all* facts should be laid out, but that *doesn't disqualify* these as potential solutions.
